annotations.text:
Where should the digits sit?

One variable only: the arcs are identical between the two rows — same −5→35 °C scale, same fill lengths. Read DOWN a column to see one reading in both treatments; read ACROSS a row to see what changing temperature does to the layout.

RIDE — the digit marks where its arc stopped, so number and bar read as one object and there is never a question which arc a number belongs to. The face feels alive.

Against: nothing sits still. Your eye has to FIND the number before it can read it, which is the opposite of what a watch glance is for. At some readings it parks under a hand — see Ride · mild, where the minute hand crosses the air digits. And with no data there is no arc end to ride: the −− has nowhere to go.

PARK — air always top, water always bottom. You learn two spots once and stop looking; the arcs become peripheral colour you read without focusing on them.

Against: the number no longer points at anything, so each arc has to earn its place on its own. At cold values a stubby arc next to a big centred digit can look disconnected — compare Park · cold.

Four directions, one axis each — A bets on illustration, B on analogue encoding, C on typography, D on cutting the face down to one question.

All five are drawn true size (260 × 260, gabbro) at 10:09, air 24°, Aare 19°, so they compare directly. B is the chosen direction; it is developed on the Twin Arc page.

Every colour is on Pebble's 64-value palette, so all of this is drawable on-device:

FFFFFF / AAAAAA / 555555 · FFAA00 air · 00AAFF Aare · 5555AA deep water · 00FFAA swim-good · 555500 + 005555 gauge tracks.

Type is a stand-in — on-device this is the Gothic bitmap set (14 / 18) plus LECO numerals for the big readouts in C and D.
